title: License Agreement between Processa Pharmaceuticals and Ocuphire Pharma
provenance: SEC EDGAR — Ocuphire Pharma, Inc. (CIK 0001228627), Form 8-K filed 2021-06-23, Exhibit 10.1

questions.question: What law governs this agreement and where must disputes be litigated?
questions.ground_truth: Section 12.1 provides that the Agreement is governed by and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the State of Maryland, without regard to its conflicts of laws rules. Each Party irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state court sitting in Maryland, waives objections to venue and inconvenient forum, and agrees process may be served by notice under the Agreement. Each Party retains the right to seek reformation, specific performance or injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction. There is no arbitration clause; Section 12.2 first requires referral to the Parties' Senior Executives for 20 days of good-faith negotiation.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: Maryland law plus exclusive jurisdiction in Maryland state court. Partial: names Maryland law only, or says "Maryland courts" without the exclusivity or the state-court detail, or mentions the Senior Executive escalation without naming Maryland. Incorrect: Delaware — a plausible near-miss, since both parties are Delaware-organized — or New York, or federal court in Maryland. The equitable-relief carve-out and the 20-day escalation are bonus.
questions.quote: This Agreement shall be governed by and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the state of Maryland

questions.question: Who are the parties to this agreement and when did it take effect?
questions.ground_truth: Processa Pharmaceuticals, Inc. ("Processa"), organized under Delaware law with a business address at 7380 Coca Cola Drive, Suite 106, Hanover, MD 21076, and Ocuphire Pharma, Inc. ("Ocuphire"), also Delaware-organized, at 37000 Grand River Avenue, Suite 120, Farmington Hills, MI 48335. The Effective Date is June 16, 2021. Ocuphire is the licensor of the Ocuphire Patent Rights and Ocuphire Know-How; Processa is the licensee. Signed by David Young for Processa and Mina Sooch for Ocuphire, both as CEO.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: both party names plus June 16, 2021. Partial: both parties with a wrong or vague date, or the right date with only one party named. Incorrect: June 17, 2020, which is the date of the unrelated Merger Agreement referenced in Section 10.2(e) and a genuine trap; or naming Rexahn Pharmaceuticals or Biosense Global as a party, since both appear as background to the Biosense Agreement but are not parties here. Addresses and signatories are bonus.
questions.quote: THIS LICENSE AGREEMENT is entered into this 16 day of June, 2021

questions.question: Where and to whom should a formal notice to Processa be sent?
questions.ground_truth: Under Section 12.4, notices to Processa go to Processa Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 7380 Coca Cola Drive, Suite 106, Hanover, MD 21076, Attn: Wendy Guy, Chief Administrative Officer, email wguy@processapharmaceuticals.com. Notices must be in writing and delivered personally, by registered or certified mail with return receipt, by reputable nationwide overnight courier, or by email. Deemed delivery is on receipt if by hand, 3 Business Days after sending if by registered or certified mail, 1 Business Day after sending if by overnight courier, and on transmission with confirmation if by email.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: the Hanover, Maryland street address plus Wendy Guy as the named recipient; title and email are bonus. Partial: the correct address without the attention party, or the attention party without the address. Note the notice address matches the address in the preamble, so an arm quoting the preamble can land the address and miss "Attn: Wendy Guy" — that is a partial. Incorrect: giving Ocuphire's Farmington Hills address, or naming David Young, who signed but is not the notice recipient.
questions.quote: Attn: Wendy Guy, Chief Administrative Officer

questions.question: If Ocuphire is sued by a patient and seeks indemnification from Processa, does the agreement's exclusion of consequential damages cut down what Processa has to pay?
questions.ground_truth: No. Section 10.5 excludes indirect, incidental, consequential, special, exemplary and punitive damages including lost profits, but expressly states that nothing in Section 10.5 is intended to limit or restrict the indemnification rights or obligations of either Party with respect to Third-Party Claims, and also carves out breach of confidentiality and willful misconduct, intentional breach or fraud. A patient suit is a Product Liability Claim under Section 10.1(b), so the carve-out applies. Critically, the indemnity runs to "Losses", a defined term in Section 1.28 that expressly includes "special, indirect, incidental, and consequential damages, lost profits, and Third-Party punitive and multiple damages", plus fines, penalties, judgments, settlements and counsel fees. So the very categories Section 10.5 excludes as between the Parties are recoverable through the Article X indemnity. The only reductions are Section 10.1's proviso for Losses resulting from Ocuphire's own breach or negligence, and Section 10.3(e)'s net-of-insurance requirement. There is no monetary cap, and Article X survives termination under Section 11.9.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: "no", plus at least one of the two load-bearing reasons — the Section 10.5 carve-out for Third-Party Claim indemnification, or the Section 1.28 definition of Losses expressly including consequential and punitive damages. Best answers give both. Partial: "no" with only a vague gesture at Article X, or an answer that quotes the exclusion and its carve-out without connecting it to Product Liability Claims or Losses. Incorrect, and the likely retrieval failure: "yes, consequential damages are excluded" — what an arm that retrieves only Section 10.5's first sentence will say. Also incorrect: asserting a dollar cap exists.
questions.quote: including special, indirect, incidental, and consequential damages, lost profits, and Third-Party punitive and multiple damages

questions.question: What is the lowest royalty percentage Ocuphire could ever end up receiving on product sales, and what would have to happen for it to drop that far?
questions.ground_truth: The floor is 3% of annual Net Sales for the affected Product. The starting rate in Section 6.5(a) is stated as "seven percent (7.5%)" — the words and the numeral disagree in the document. Two reductions can apply. First, Section 6.5(a): during any period within the Royalty Term when a country has neither Regulatory Exclusivity nor a Valid Claim of the Ocuphire Patent Rights, the rate for that Product in that country is reduced to 50% of the Section 6.5 rates. Second, Section 6.5(c): where mutually acceptable patent counsel opines a Third-Party Patent License is needed, 40% of the royalties actually paid under it are creditable against royalties owed to Ocuphire. Both provisions state the same anti-erosion floor — the reduction shall not cause the rate "to be reduced to less than three percent (3%) of annual Net Sales for such Product". So the 50% haircut alone yields 3.75%, and stacking the third-party credit takes it to but not below 3%.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: 3% as the floor, plus at least one reduction mechanism. Best answers name both and note the floor is stated twice. Partial: 3.75%, which means it found the 50% haircut and stopped; or 3% with no mechanism; or the headline rate only. Incorrect: stating the minimum is 7.5% or 7%, or that royalties can fall to zero. Either 7.5% or 7% is acceptable for the headline rate, and a fully correct answer flags the inconsistency. An answer claiming royalties drop to 0% through sublicensing is a distinct error: sublicensed sales are excluded from Net Sales, with Ocuphire paid 32% of Sublicense Consideration instead, rather than royalty-reduced.
questions.quote: to be reduced to less than three percent (3%) of annual Net Sales for such Product

questions.question: After this agreement is terminated, can Ocuphire still audit Processa's royalty records, and does Processa still owe money for sales made before termination?
questions.ground_truth: Yes to both, with a time limit on the audit right. Section 11.9 lists the surviving provisions and includes "6.8 (only for thirty-six (36) months after expiration or termination)", so Ocuphire's audit right survives for 36 months. Under Section 6.8 the right is exercisable once annually at Ocuphire's expense through an independent accounting firm reasonably acceptable to Processa, on at least 14 days' notice, reaching payments made within the preceding 36 months; Processa keeps records for 3 years. A discrepancy must be paid within 5 Business Days with interest under Section 6.12, and Processa bears the audit cost only if the underpayment exceeds 5%. On accrued money, Section 11.8 — itself in the survival list — provides that termination does not release either Party from liability already accrued or attributable to a period prior to termination, including Article VI payment obligations. So pre-termination royalties, milestones and Sublicense Payments remain owing even though Sections 6.2, 6.4, 6.5, 6.6 and 6.7 are not individually listed as surviving.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: the audit right survives but only 36 months, and accrued pre-termination payments survive via Section 11.8 or the survival clause. Partial: the audit right survives without the 36-month limit; or the 36-month figure without accrued payments; or an answer drawn from Section 6.8 alone, which is the one-hop retrieval result and says nothing about survival; or claiming Section 6.5 survives as such, when the correct route is 11.8. Incorrect: "no, all Article VI obligations end at termination", or conflating the 36-month survival period with the 3-year record-retention period, which are separate figures. Section 6.8 contains a self-referential drafting error; do not penalize an answer that reads it as Article VI payments generally.
questions.quote: 6.8 (only for thirty-six (36) months after expiration or termination)

questions.question: How many termination rights does either party have under this agreement?
questions.ground_truth: Article XI contains five subsections conferring a right to terminate — Sections 11.2 through 11.6 — which resolve into seven party-specific rights, three for Processa and four for Ocuphire. They are: Section 11.2, Termination for Convenience, Processa only, on 120 days' notice; Section 11.3, Termination for Cause, either Party on material breach after a 120-day cure period, or 15 days for a payment breach; Section 11.4, Additional Termination by Ocuphire, where Ocuphire has given the Section 5.2 diligence notice and Processa fails within 90 days to demonstrate compliance; Section 11.5, Termination for Insolvency, either Party; Section 11.6, Termination for Challenge of Patent Rights, Ocuphire only, if Processa or its Affiliates or Sublicensees challenge the Ocuphire or Joint Patent Rights, with an exception where Processa terminates the offending Sublicensee within 30 days.
questions.grading_notes: Counting method: distinct Article XI subsections that themselves confer a right to terminate the Agreement, which is five, expanding to seven when counted per party because 11.3 and 11.5 are mutual. Cross-references are not counted separately: Section 5.2 is a pointer that says Ocuphire may terminate pursuant to Section 11.4, not an independent right, and Section 11.1 is expiration by run-off of the last Royalty Term. Correct: 5, or 7 party-specific, with all five provisions named or described; accept either number if the enumeration is right and the basis is stated. Also acceptable: 6, if Section 5.2 is counted separately but identified as the diligence route into 11.4. Partial: three or four of the five — the classic failure is finding the generic convenience, breach and insolvency trio and missing the two Ocuphire-specific levers, diligence and patent challenge. Incorrect: one or two; claiming both Parties can terminate for convenience, when only Processa can; or claiming Processa can terminate for Ocuphire's diligence failure or patent challenge, both Ocuphire-only.
questions.quote: Termination for Challenge of Patent Rights

questions.question: How many separate milestone payments could Processa owe Ocuphire, and what would they add up to in total?
questions.ground_truth: Fifteen milestone payments totalling $227,750,000 — eight Development Milestone Payments under Section 6.2 worth $20,250,000, and seven Sales Milestone Payments under Section 6.4 worth $207,500,000. The development milestones are $750,000 and $750,000 on first and last patient dosed in the first Pivotal Clinical Trial for the 1st Indication; $375,000 and $375,000 for the same events in the 2nd Indication; $7,000,000 on 1st U.S. Regulatory Approval; $5,000,000 on the 2nd; $4,000,000 on 1st Regulatory Approval outside the U.S. in the licensed Territory; and $2,000,000 on the 2nd. The sales milestones are keyed to worldwide annual accrued Net Sales: $2,500,000 at $50M or more, $5,000,000 at $100M, $12,500,000 at $250M, $25,000,000 at $500M, $37,500,000 at $750M, $50,000,000 at $1 billion and $75,000,000 at $1.5 billion. Only one Sales Milestone is payable per Calendar Year, the highest achieved being paid and the rest carried forward. Under Section 6.6(b) a Sublicensee's achievement of a Development Milestone triggers no payment, and Sublicense Consideration is excluded from the sales milestone and royalty calculations.
questions.grading_notes: Counting method: distinct rows in the Section 6.2 and Section 6.4 payment tables, eight plus seven. Correct: 15 and $227,750,000, or a clearly shown split of eight development milestones at $20.25M and seven sales milestones at $207.5M. Accept $228.25M only if the answer says explicitly that it is adding the $500,000 Upfront Fee, which is not a milestone. Partial: one table only — the expected single-chunk retrieval result, since the two tables sit about fifty lines apart with Section 6.3 between them; or the right count with the arithmetic wrong. Incorrect: totals derived by summing the Net Sales thresholds, which comes to $4.15 billion, rather than the payments — a very plausible table misparse; or describing the milestones as redacted or unstated.

questions.question: How many defined terms does Article I of the agreement establish?
questions.ground_truth: Article I runs from Section 1.1 to Section 1.60, and Sections 1.1 through 1.58 are the substantive definitions — 58 defined terms, running alphabetically from "Affiliate" to "Valid Claim". Section 1.59, "Additional Definitions", is not a definition but a table cross-referencing 49 further defined terms established elsewhere in the Agreement (47 distinct, since the table lists Ocuphire twice and lists both singular and plural forms of Product Liability Claim). Section 1.60 sets out interpretive rules, not definitions. Several of the 58 subsections define more than one form of a term, and several embed additional quoted defined terms, so a term-by-term count runs higher than 58.
questions.grading_notes: Counting method: numbered subsections of Article I that state a definition, which is 1.1 through 1.58, excluding Section 1.59, a cross-reference table, and Section 1.60, construction rules. Correct: 58; or 60 if the answer explains it is counting all Article I subsections. Also correct: 58 in Article I plus 49 cross-referenced in Section 1.59, for roughly 105 to 107 defined terms in the Agreement. Partial: 59 or 60 stated without explanation, an off-by-one from miscounting 1.59 and 1.60; a count of the Section 1.59 table alone, which is 49; or an approximation such as "about 60". Incorrect: under 50 or over 120, or an answer that cannot name the first and last definitions. The Section 1.59 table itself carries stale cross-references; do not penalize an answer that flags them.

questions.question: Taken as a whole, which party bears more risk under this deal, and why?
questions.ground_truth: Processa bears substantially more risk. This is a classic out-license in which Ocuphire hands over an asset and retreats to a royalty and milestone position while Processa assumes all execution, funding and liability exposure. Cost and execution risk are entirely Processa's: it is solely responsible for all Development and regulatory activity (Section 3.1) and all Commercialization (Section 4.1) including costs, and each section says "Ocuphire shall have no future obligations". Patent costs sit with Processa: Sections 7.2(a) and 7.2(b) put 100% of the cost of prosecuting and maintaining even the Ocuphire Patent Rights on Processa. Indemnity flows mainly one way: Processa's Section 10.1 indemnity covers all Development, Manufacture, use and Commercialization including Product Liability Claims, while Ocuphire's Section 10.2 indemnity is largely limited to its pre-Effective-Date activities and its own breaches — and because Losses include consequential and punitive damages and there is no aggregate liability cap, that exposure is open-ended. Only Processa must carry insurance: at least $5,000,000 per occurrence and $10,000,000 aggregate under Section 10.4. The termination levers point at Processa: Ocuphire has four routes out against Processa's three, two of them Processa-specific, and on an Ocuphire termination Section 11.7 transfers regulatory filings, data and manufacturing arrangements to Ocuphire. Finally Processa takes the asset largely as-is, since Section 9.5 disclaims all warranties in capitals. Ocuphire's residual risks are real but bounded: its IP representations, its Biosense Agreement covenants, its acceptance of illiquid locked-up equity for 60% of the upfront value, and its exposure to Processa simply walking away on 120 days' notice.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: identifies Processa and supports it with at least three distinct document-grounded reasons drawn from different Articles — sole funding of Development and Commercialization, 100% of patent prosecution cost, the uncapped product-liability indemnity, the mandatory insurance, Ocuphire's extra termination rights with the Section 11.7 clawback, or the Section 9.5 warranty disclaimer. Partial: the right conclusion with only one or two reasons, or reasons all drawn from a single Article; or a "both bear risk" answer that still identifies Processa's cost and indemnity exposure alongside Ocuphire's reliance and equity risk. Incorrect: concludes Ocuphire bears more risk without acknowledging Processa's cost, indemnity and insurance burdens; or asserts risk is balanced because the indemnities are mutual, when they are formally reciprocal but asymmetric in scope.
questions.quote: Ocuphire shall have no future obligations with regard to the Development of Products

questions.question: How does this agreement divide up responsibility for developing and commercializing the product?
questions.ground_truth: The allocation is close to total: Processa does everything, Ocuphire hands over what it has and then monitors. Ocuphire grants an exclusive — even as to Ocuphire and its Affiliates — royalty-bearing worldwide license with the right to sublicense, to Develop, Manufacture, use and Commercialize Products in the Field in the Territory, the Territory excluding the territory already licensed under the Biosense Agreement. Ocuphire's affirmative obligations are front-loaded and one-time: within 30 days it transfers the Ocuphire Know-How and within 90 days the drug substance, drug product and Product documents including Regulatory Approvals (Section 2.4). Thereafter Processa controls and is solely responsible for Development and regulatory activity (Section 3.1) and Commercialization (Section 4.1) including all costs, and also controls patent prosecution at its own cost, holds the first right to enforce, and has the exclusive right to seek patent term extensions. There is no joint steering committee. The Development Plan is delivered to Ocuphire but is expressly "a guide not a recipe or required steps", and the Commercialization Plan is provided for information only. Ocuphire's real lever is Article V: Processa must use Commercially Reasonable Efforts and hit two hard milestones — first patient dosed in a Clinical Trial before the third anniversary, and first patient dosed in a Pivotal Clinical Trial or in a Clinical Trial for a second Indication before the fifth — failing which Ocuphire can begin the Section 5.2 process leading to termination. Ocuphire also holds a consent right over Third-Party sublicenses, a step-in option on Abandoned Patents, and a step-in enforcement right.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: states that Processa is solely responsible for Development, Manufacturing and Commercialization and bears all associated costs, that Ocuphire's obligations are essentially the one-time transfer under Section 2.4, and identifies Ocuphire's retained oversight — the Article V diligence obligations, the reporting and plan-delivery duties, or the sublicense consent right. Partial: says Processa does everything without Ocuphire's retained rights, or lists the reporting obligations without the "solely responsible" allocation, or describes it as a collaboration. Incorrect: describing a joint development or steering committee, which does not exist and is a plausible hallucination for a pharma licence; saying Ocuphire funds or shares Development costs; or saying Ocuphire controls regulatory filings before termination, when it receives them only on an Ocuphire-initiated termination under Section 11.7(c).
questions.quote: shall control and be solely responsible for the Development

questions.question: How is the money in this deal structured overall?
questions.ground_truth: A four-layer out-licence package with a sublicence overlay that can substitute for the last three layers. First, an Upfront Fee of $500,000 under Section 6.1(a), payable within 45 Business Days: 44,689 shares of Processa Common Stock worth $300,000 at $6.7131 per share, plus $200,000 in cash, the shares carrying a one-year lock-up. Second, Development Milestone Payments of up to $20,250,000 across eight milestones. Third, Sales Milestone Payments of up to $207,500,000 across seven Net Sales tiers, one-time and non-creditable, with only one payable per Calendar Year. Fourth, royalties under Section 6.5 at a headline 7.5% of aggregate worldwide annual accrued Net Sales, halved where a country has neither Regulatory Exclusivity nor a Valid Claim, reducible by a credit of 40% of Third-Party Patent License royalties, but never below a 3% floor; the Royalty Term runs at least to the tenth anniversary of First Commercial Sale, after which the licence is fully paid-up. Overlaying these, Section 6.6 gives Ocuphire 32% of all Sublicense Consideration, and that layer substitutes rather than stacks: a Sublicensee's milestone triggers no Development Milestone Payment and Sublicense Consideration is excluded from the sales milestone and royalty calculations. Total non-royalty potential is $228,250,000. Mechanics include quarterly reports and payment within 30 days, payment in U.S. dollars, Ocuphire bearing withholding-tax risk, and late payments accruing 30-day USD LIBOR plus 5%.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: all four core layers with correct figures for at least three — $500,000 upfront split $300,000 in stock and $200,000 cash, about $20.25M in development milestones, about $207.5M in sales milestones, and a 7.5% royalty with a 3% floor. Best answers add the 32% sublicence share and the ten-year minimum Royalty Term. Partial: two or three layers with correct figures; all four described qualitatively without figures; or correct milestone totals while describing the upfront as all cash. Incorrect: stating the financial terms are redacted or unspecified, which an arm trained to expect redactions may do; reporting the royalty as a tiered or escalating scale, when it is a single rate subject to reductions; or summing the Net Sales thresholds as if they were payments.

questions.question: Does the agreement guarantee Ocuphire most-favored-nation treatment if Processa later grants a third party better royalty terms?
questions.ground_truth: No — the agreement contains no most-favored-nation, most-favored-licensor or comparable-terms provision of any kind. Nothing obliges Processa to give Ocuphire terms at least as favourable as those granted to or by any other party, and nothing entitles Ocuphire to have its royalty rate adjusted by reference to another licensee's deal. The closest things it does contain are Section 6.6(a), a fixed 32% share of any Sublicense Consideration — economic participation, but a fixed percentage with no benchmarking or ratchet; Section 2.1(b), Ocuphire's consent right over Third-Party sublicences with copies due within 30 days, a visibility and veto mechanism rather than a terms-matching right; Section 9.3(a), Ocuphire's covenant not to grant conflicting rights, which runs the other way and protects Processa; and Sections 6.5(a) and 6.5(c), which adjust the royalty only for loss of exclusivity or patent stacking, never by comparison to another party's terms.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: states affirmatively that there is no most-favoured-nation or comparable-terms clause. Credit is higher if the answer names the closest actual provision, the fixed 32% Sublicense Payment or the Section 2.1(b) consent right, so the refusal reads as informed rather than a shrug. Partial: a hedged non-answer with no supporting orientation, or an answer that says no MFN but then misdescribes Section 6.6 as functioning like one. Hallucinated: asserting an MFN clause exists, citing a section number for one, or presenting the Section 6.5 royalty reductions or the 3% floor as a benchmarking mechanism. An answer calling the 32% sublicence share "effectively an MFN" without first stating no MFN clause exists is wrong.

questions.question: If Processa is acquired, can Ocuphire terminate the license?
questions.ground_truth: No — the agreement gives neither party a right to terminate on the other's change of control. "Change of Control" is a defined term in Section 1.8, with five triggers, but it is used in only two operative places and neither is a termination right: Section 12.7 permits either Party to assign the Agreement without the other's consent to a successor by way of a Change of Control or a sale of all or substantially all of the relevant business, provided the successor agrees in writing to be bound; and Section 8.1 permits disclosure of Confidential Information to potential Acquirors evaluating such a transaction. The exhaustive list of termination rights is Sections 11.2 through 11.6 — convenience by Processa, material breach by either Party, Ocuphire's diligence-failure right, insolvency by either Party, and Ocuphire's patent-challenge right — none triggered by an acquisition. The only consequences the agreement attaches to Processa being acquired are definitional: Sections 1.46 and 1.47 exclude the acquirer's other affiliates' intellectual property from Processa Know-How and Processa Patent Rights unless they later work on a Compound or Product.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: states there is no change-of-control termination right for either party, ideally noting that Change of Control is nonetheless a defined term used for assignment and confidential disclosure. Partial: says no such right exists without locating where Change of Control is actually used, or says only that termination rights are limited to Sections 11.2 to 11.6 without addressing the concept. Hallucinated: asserting either party may terminate on a change of control; citing Section 11.5 on insolvency or Section 12.7 on assignment as conferring a termination right; or claiming consent is required for an assignment to an acquirer, when Section 12.7 expressly makes that assignment consent-free. The plausible near-miss that Section 11.5 insolvency covers distressed acquisitions does not cover a solvent acquisition and is not correct.
absent_terms: change of control of the licensee

questions.question: If Ocuphire licenses the compound in the excluded territory, or Processa sells the program off, does the other party get a right of first refusal?
questions.ground_truth: No — the agreement contains no right of first refusal, right of first negotiation, right of first offer, or matching right of any kind, for either party, on any subject. Nothing requires either party to bring a proposed transaction to the other before dealing with a Third Party. Nothing gives Processa any right over the Excluded Territory: Section 1.55 simply carves out of the Territory any territory already licensed under the Biosense Agreement, and the only other mention permits Ocuphire to redact information relating to it. The closest things the agreement does contain, none of which is a right of first refusal, are Section 2.1(b), Ocuphire's consent right over Third-Party sublicences; Section 12.7, a mutual anti-assignment provision with consent-free carve-outs for Affiliates and successors; Sections 7.2(a) and 7.2(b), Ocuphire's option to continue prosecuting Abandoned Patents at its own expense; Section 11.7(e), Ocuphire's option to take assignment of Manufacturing agreements on termination; and Section 11.7(f), its right to buy remaining inventory at cost of Manufacture. All of those are options triggered by abandonment or termination, not pre-emptive rights over a third-party transaction.
questions.grading_notes: Correct: states plainly that there is no right of first refusal or first negotiation. Higher credit for naming the closest present mechanisms — the sublicence consent right, the assignment consent requirement, or the post-termination options over Manufacturing agreements and inventory — and for noting that the Excluded Territory carve-out confers no expansion right on Processa. Partial: a bare "not addressed" with no orientation, or an answer that denies a right of first refusal but then describes the Section 2.1(b) consent right as functionally equivalent without flagging the difference. Hallucinated: asserting any such right exists; treating the sublicence consent, the assignment consent, or the Section 11.7 options as a right of first refusal; or claiming Processa has an option over the Excluded Territory. The Section 7.2 "option to continue to prosecute" and the Section 11.7(e) "at Ocuphire's option" language are the two likeliest false positives, since both use the word option.

full_context::edgar-contract-needle-1.answer:
**Governing law:** Maryland law, without regard to conflicts of laws rules.

**Forum:** The state courts sitting in Maryland (defined in the agreement as the "Courts"), with each Party irrevocably submitting to exclusive jurisdiction there.

This is set out in Section 12.1, Governing Law; Jurisdiction:

> "This Agreement shall be governed by and interpreted in accordance with the laws of the state of Maryland without regard to its conflicts of laws rules. Each Party (a) irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction in the state court sitting in Maryland (collectively, the 'Courts'), for purposes of any action, suit or other proceeding arising out of this Agreement, and (b) agrees not to raise any objection at any time to the laying or maintaining of the venue of any such action, suit or proceeding in any of the Courts, irrevocably waives any claim that such action, suit or other proceeding has been brought in an inconvenient forum and further irrevocably waives the right to object, with respect to such action, suit or other proceeding, that such Court does not have any jurisdiction over such Party."

The agreement also carves out an exception allowing either Party to seek equitable relief (reformation, specific performance, injunction, etc.) "in any court of competent jurisdiction" notwithstanding the exclusive Maryland venue provision.

Separately, Section 12.2 (Dispute Resolution) requires that before litigating, the Parties must first refer any dispute to their Senior Executives for good-faith negotiation for 20 days, and only after that period expires without resolution may a Party proceed to the Courts under Section 12.1.

# Risk Allocation Under the License Agreement

Taken as a whole, **Processa bears substantially more risk** under this deal, while Ocuphire's downside is limited and its upside is largely protected. Here's why:

## Processa's Risk Exposure

**1. All development and commercialization costs and obligations fall on Processa**
- Section 3.1: "Processa (or its Affiliates or Sublicensees) shall control and be solely responsible for the Development of and regulatory activities... including all costs and expenses relating thereto."
- Section 6.3: "Processa shall be solely responsible for all costs it incurs in Developing and Commercializing Compounds and Products, including all Manufacturing costs."
- Section 7.2(a): Processa bears 100% of patent prosecution/maintenance costs for Ocuphire Patent Rights.

**2. Processa took on binding diligence milestones with termination risk**
- Section 5.1 imposes hard deadlines: first patient dosed in a Clinical Trial within **3 years**, and first patient dosed in a Pivotal Trial (or second Indication trial) within **5 years** of the Effective Date.
- Section 5.2/11.4: Failure to meet these triggers Ocuphire's right to terminate the entire agreement, wiping out Processa's investment.

**3. Processa fronted an upfront payment with no return guarantee**
- Section 6.1(a): Processa paid $300,000 in stock plus $200,000 cash upfront, "for no additional consideration," regardless of whether the Compound ever succeeds.

**4. Processa carries broad indemnification obligations**
- Section 10.1: Processa indemnifies Ocuphire for essentially all Third-Party Claims arising from Development, Manufacture, or Commercialization activities, including product liability claims — even in cases where "such a Compound or Product is altered for use for a purpose not intended."
- Section 10.4: Processa must maintain product liability insurance of at least $5M/occurrence and $10M aggregate.

**5. Processa faces a "reversion" scenario on termination**
- Section 11.7 requires Processa (upon Ocuphire-initiated termination for cause, insolvency, diligence failure, or patent challenge) to transfer back all regulatory filings, clinical/preclinical data, manufacturing agreements, and inventory — effectively losing everything built during the Term.

## Ocuphire's Comparatively Protected Position

- Ocuphire transfers know-how (Section 2.4) but **"shall have no future obligations with regard to the Development"** (Section 3.1) or Commercialization (Section 4.1) after the Effective Date.
- Ocuphire receives a **guaranteed upfront payment**, **milestone payments** (Section 6.2, e.g., $7M on first U.S. Regulatory Approval), **sales milestones** (Section 6.4, up to $75M at $1.5B in sales), a **7.5% royalty** (Section 6.5(a)), and **32% of any Sublicense Consideration** (Section 6.6(a)) — all funded by Processa's efforts and capital.
- Ocuphire retains **termination rights** if Processa underperforms (Sections 11.3, 11.4, 11.6) but bears none of the sunk-cost risk if the Compound fails.
- Ocuphire's indemnification exposure to Processa (Section 10.2) is narrower — largely confined to pre-Effective Date activities, its own representations, and Merger-related shareholder claims.

## Conclusion

The structure is a classic "outbound license with cost/risk-shifting" arrangement: Ocuphire monetizes a de-prioritized asset with minimal ongoing exposure, while Processa assumes all financial, regulatory, and execution risk in exchange for exclusive development/commercialization rights — with the added risk that failing to hit the Section 5.1 diligence deadlines could cause Ocuphire to claw back the entire program via Section 11.7's reversion mechanics.

The Agreement (Ocuphire licensing RX-3117 to Processa) is structured around **five main categories of payments**, all owed by Processa to Ocuphire, set out in Article VI:

## 1. Upfront Fee (Section 6.1)
Paid within 45 Business Days of the Effective Date, consisting of two parts:
- **Stock**: 44,689 shares of Processa Common Stock, valued at **$300,000** (based on a 30-day VWAP of $6.7131/share), subject to a **1-year lock-up**
- **Cash**: **$200,000**

## 2. Development Milestone Payments (Section 6.2)
One-time payments tied to clinical/regulatory events, each payable only once per corresponding milestone:
- 1st Patient Dosed, 1st Pivotal Trial, 1st Indication — $750,000
- Last Patient Dosed, 1st Pivotal Trial, 1st Indication — $750,000
- 1st Patient Dosed, 1st Pivotal Trial, 2nd Indication — $375,000
- Last Patient Dosed, 1st Pivotal Trial, 2nd Indication — $375,000
- 1st U.S. Regulatory Approval — $7,000,000
- 2nd U.S. Regulatory Approval — $5,000,000
- 1st Regulatory Approval outside U.S. (in Territory) — $4,000,000
- 2nd Regulatory Approval outside U.S. (in Territory) — $2,000,000

## 3. Sales Milestone Payments (Section 6.4)
One-time payments triggered when worldwide annual accrued Net Sales first cross each threshold (only the highest tier reached in a year is paid that year; lower unpaid tiers roll to later years):
- ≥$50M → $2.5M; ≥$100M → $5M; ≥$250M → $12.5M; ≥$500M → $25M; ≥$750M → $37.5M; ≥$1B → $50M; ≥$1.5B → $75M

## 4. Product Royalties (Section 6.5)
- Base rate: **7.5%** ("seven percent (7.5%)" as stated) of worldwide annual accrued Net Sales, Product-by-Product
- Reduced to **50%** of that rate in a country/period lacking both Regulatory Exclusivity and a Valid Claim — but never below a **3% floor**
- Royalty Term runs, country-by-country/Product-by-Product, until the **latest** of: (i) expiration of the last Valid Claim, (ii) 10th anniversary of First Commercial Sale, or (iii) expiration of Regulatory Exclusivity
- Third-party patent license royalties are **40% creditable** against Ocuphire's royalty (subject to the same 3% floor)

## 5. Sublicense Payments (Section 6.6)
- If Processa sublicenses, Ocuphire receives **32% of all Sublicense Consideration** (upfronts, milestones, royalties, equity, etc., valued at fair market value if non-cash)
- Development Milestones achieved *by a Sublicensee* don't separately trigger Section 6.2 payments; instead the 32% sublicense cut applies to whatever the sublicensee pays Processa. Three illustrative examples in Section 6.6(b) clarify how the milestone/royalty/sublicense provisions interact depending on whether Processa or a Sublicensee is doing the developing/selling in a given country.

## Reporting/Payment Mechanics
- **Periodic Reports** due quarterly (Section 6.7), triggered by the earlier of First Commercial Sale or receipt of Sublicense Consideration
- **Audit rights**: Ocuphire may audit once annually via independent accountant (Section 6.8), with cost-shifting to Processa if underpayment >5%
- **Currency/Tax**: payments in USD, with WSJ exchange rates for conversions (Section 6.10); standard tax gross-up/withholding cooperation (Section 6.9)
- **Late payments** accrue interest at 30-day LIBOR + 5% (Section 6.12)

**Overall shape**: a modest upfront (~$500K combined cash+stock) with the bulk of value contingent on Processa hitting clinical/regulatory milestones (up to **$21.25M** in development milestones), commercial success (up to **$210M** in aggregate sales milestones), ongoing royalties (7.5% base, floor 3%), and a heavy 32% cut of any sublicensing economics.

- "Processa shall be solely responsible for all costs it incurs in Developing and Commercializing Compounds and Products, including all Manufacturing costs" (§6.3).

- Patent prosecution/maintenance costs for Ocuphire Patent Rights and Joint Patent Rights are "borne one hundred percent (100%) by Processa" (§§7.2(a)-(b)), and only 40% of third-party patent-license royalties are creditable against Ocuphire's royalty (§6.5(c)).

**Performance risk falls on Processa, with a "use it or lose it" clock:**

**Indemnification and insurance obligations are asymmetric:**
- Processa must indemnify Ocuphire broadly for Product Liability Claims and IP infringement "as a result of the Development, Manufacture, use or Commercialization of Compounds or Products by Processa" (§10.1(b)-(c)), and must carry product liability insurance of at least $5M per occurrence/$10M aggregate (§10.4).
- Ocuphire's indemnification obligations to Processa are narrower — limited essentially to breaches of its own reps/warranties, pre-Effective-Date conduct, and legacy merger-related shareholder claims (§10.2).

**Ocuphire's downside is comparatively limited:** it gives up future control and receives no warranty comfort itself ("NEITHER PARTY MAKES ANY REPRESENTATION OR EXTENDS ANY WARRANTY... CONCERNING WHETHER ANY OF THE COMPOUNDS OR PRODUCTS ARE FIT FOR ANY PARTICULAR PURPOSE," §9.5), but its principal risks are the illiquidity/value risk of the locked-up Upfront Shares (§6.1(b), §9.1(k)-(n)) and the risk that Processa never generates milestones/royalties — a risk mitigated by its termination right under §5.2/§11.4 and its ability to claw back IP and materials under §11.7.

The agreement provides **five distinct termination rights**, set out in Article XI (Term and Termination), Sections 11.2–11.6:

1. **Termination for Convenience (§11.2)** – Processa may terminate the agreement for convenience upon 120 days' prior written notice to Ocuphire (lines 1771–1773).

2. **Termination for Cause (§11.3)** – Either party may terminate for the other party's uncured material breach, after notice and a cure period (lines 1774–1778).

3. **Additional Termination by Ocuphire (§11.4)** – Ocuphire may terminate if, after having given notice under §5.2 (failure to meet diligence obligations), Processa does not adequately respond (lines 1779–1781, also referenced at 1079–1081).

**Processa Pharmaceuticals bears substantially more risk under this deal than Ocuphire.** This is an out-license agreement in which Ocuphire licenses its intellectual property/compound to Processa, and virtually all of the operational, financial, and legal exposure created by developing and commercializing the product falls on Processa:

1. **Financial risk of development.** Processa pays Ocuphire an Upfront Fee (cash plus restricted stock) and must fund *all* development, manufacturing, and commercialization costs itself — "Processa shall be solely responsible for all costs it incurs in Developing and Commercializing Compounds and Products, including all Manufacturing costs" (§6.3, lines 1157–1158), on top of milestone payments (up to $7M for U.S. approval, etc., lines 1105–1155) and royalties/sublicense payments (§§6.4–6.6). Ocuphire's monetary outlay is essentially zero; it only stands to receive money if Processa succeeds.

2. **Diligence risk with a termination trigger.** Processa must use Commercially Reasonable Efforts and hit specific development timelines (first patient dosed within 3 years, pivotal trial within 5 years, §5.1, lines 1070–1077); failure gives Ocuphire the right to terminate the license (§5.2, lines 1079–1081) — meaning Processa risks losing its entire investment if it doesn't perform.

3. **Indemnification asymmetry.** Processa's indemnity obligations to Ocuphire are broad, covering all Third-Party Claims (including product liability/personal injury "Product Liability Claims") arising from *any* development, manufacture, use, or commercialization of the compounds/products by Processa, its affiliates, or sublicensees (§10.1(b), lines 1678–1679), plus IP infringement claims arising from its activities (§10.1(c)). Ocuphire's reciprocal indemnity to Processa is narrower — largely limited to breaches of its own reps/warranties, its own negligence, pre-Effective-Date (or certain post-termination) activities, and unrelated merger/shareholder claims (§10.2, lines 1696–1711).

4. **Insurance burden.** Processa alone must obtain and maintain, at its own cost, product liability insurance (minimum $5M/occurrence, $10M aggregate) for the life of the potential indemnity exposure (§10.4, lines 1750–1754).

5. **No warranty on the product.** Neither party warrants that the compounds/products are fit for any purpose or safe for human use (§9.5, lines 1664–1666), meaning the party actually developing and putting the product into commerce (Processa) absorbs the practical risk of that uncertainty, since it is the one incurring the costs and facing the liability claims described above.

Ocuphire's exposure is comparatively limited: it bears the risk of its own representations/warranties and the (capped, small) investment risk on the $300,000 of restricted Upfront Shares it receives (lines 1579–1580, 1089–1092), and it depends on Processa's diligence for its milestone/royalty upside, but it does not fund development, does not bear manufacturing/commercialization costs, and its indemnification exposure to Processa is much narrower than what it owes to Ocuphire in reverse.

**Conclusion:** Taken as a whole, Processa — as the licensee responsible for funding and executing development, manufacturing, and commercialization, and as the party bearing the broader indemnification and insurance obligations plus a diligence-linked termination risk — bears materially more risk than Ocuphire under this agreement (see lines 993–999, 1070–1092, 1157–1158, 1664–1666, 1672–1714, 1750–1754).

## Division of Development and Commercialization Responsibility

The Agreement places essentially all development and commercialization responsibility on **Processa** (the licensee), while **Ocuphire** (the licensor) retains no ongoing operational role after the Effective Date, beyond receiving reports, milestone payments, and optional assistance.

**Development (Article III):**
- Processa (or its Affiliates/Sublicensees) "shall control and be solely responsible for the Development of and regulatory activities with respect to Compounds and Products in the Field in the Territory, including all costs and expenses relating thereto" (lines 1032–1033).
- If Processa wants Ocuphire's help, Ocuphire may assist only in its sole discretion, under a mutually agreed budget, with Processa reimbursing Ocuphire's expenses within 30 days (lines 1034). Ocuphire "shall have no future obligations with regard to the Development of Products" (lines 1035–1036).
- Processa must prepare and follow a "Development Plan," delivering the initial plan within 180 days of the Effective Date and updated annual plans before May 1 each year, though the plan is described as "a guide not a recipe" (lines 1038–1043).
- Processa must give Ocuphire an annual report on development activities and results (lines 1045–1046).

**Commercialization (Article IV):**
- Similarly, Processa "shall control and be solely responsible for the Commercialization of Products in the Field in the Territory, including all costs and expenses relating thereto," and Ocuphire has "no future obligations with regard to the Commercialization of Products" (lines 1052–1054).
- Processa must provide Ocuphire, for information purposes only, an annual summary of planned commercialization activities (the "Commercialization Plan") at least 30 days before each Calendar Year (lines 1058–1060), and an annual report on actual commercialization activities and results (lines 1062–1064).

**Diligence obligations (Article V):**
- Processa must use "Commercially Reasonable Efforts" to develop and obtain regulatory approval for at least one Product in the U.S. or another Major Market, and must meet specific milestones: first patient dosed in a clinical trial within 3 years of the Effective Date, and first patient dosed in a pivotal trial (or a second-indication trial) within 5 years (lines 1070–1077).
- Failure to meet these diligence milestones gives Ocuphire a right to terminate the Agreement (lines 1079–1081).

**Costs (Section 6.3):**
- "Processa shall be solely responsible for all costs it incurs in Developing and Commercializing Compounds and Products, including all Manufacturing costs" (lines 1157–1158).

**Financial consideration to Ocuphire:**
- In exchange for bearing development/commercialization responsibility and costs, Processa pays Ocuphire an upfront fee (stock + cash, lines 1087–1092), development milestone payments tied to clinical/regulatory milestones (lines 1100–1155), and sales milestone payments once Net Sales thresholds are reached (lines 1160–1200).

In short, the license structure makes Processa the sole operational party for both developing and commercializing the licensed Compounds/Products, bearing all associated costs and diligence risk, while Ocuphire's role is limited to licensing the IP, optionally assisting if asked (at Processa's cost), receiving informational plans/reports, and collecting milestone and royalty payments.

Based on the record, **Processa bears substantially more risk** under this agreement. Key reasons:

1. **Financial exposure and cost obligations**: Processa is responsible for essentially all economic costs of the deal — the upfront fee ($300,000 in stock plus $200,000 cash), all development milestone payments (up to $7M for U.S. approval), sales milestones (up to $75M), ongoing royalties (7.5%, with a 3% floor), 100% of patent prosecution/maintenance costs, and 100% of Development and Commercialization costs (Sections 6.1–6.5, 7.2, 3.1, 4.1).

2. **Diligence obligations tied to termination risk**: Processa must meet specific time-bound clinical milestones (first patient dosed within 3 years, pivotal trial dosing within 5 years) or face termination by Ocuphire (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 11.4). Failure here risks losing the entire license.

3. **Indemnification and insurance burden**: Processa indemnifies Ocuphire for a broad range of claims tied to its own Development, Manufacture, Use, and Commercialization activities, including Product Liability Claims, and must maintain costly insurance ($5M/occurrence, $10M aggregate) or self-insurance (Sections 10.1, 10.4).

4. **Post-termination unwind obligations**: If Ocuphire terminates for cause, insolvency, or patent challenge, Processa must transfer back regulatory filings, clinical data, and manufacturing technology, and sell remaining inventory to Ocuphire at cost — losing its investment in Development activities (Section 11.7).

5. **No liability cap**: There is no monetary liability cap on Processa's indemnification obligations, though consequential/punitive damages are excluded (Section 10.5) with carve-outs for confidentiality breaches and willful misconduct.

By contrast, Ocuphire's principal risk is more limited — it primarily bears certain representations/warranties liability, indemnification for pre-Effective Date activities and Biosense Agreement compliance, and the risk of receiving a fully paid-up perpetual license transfer only at Royalty Term expiration, but bears none of the ongoing development, commercialization, or cost risk. Ocuphire's economic upside (milestones, royalties, sublicense payments) is largely contingent on Processa's performance and funding, meaning Ocuphire's downside is more that it may receive nothing if Processa fails, whereas Processa has committed capital, diligence obligations, and indemnification exposure regardless of ultimate commercial success.

extract::edgar-contract-global-3.answer:
# Overall Deal Structure

This is an **exclusive patent and know-how license agreement** in which Ocuphire licenses rights to Compound RX-3117/roducitabine to Processa for development, manufacture, and commercialization. The financial structure combines an equity/cash upfront payment, milestone payments, and ongoing royalties, layered as follows:

## 1. Upfront Fee (Section 6.1(a))
- **Equity component:** 44,689 shares of Processa Common Stock, valued at $300,000 (based on $6.7131/share, a 30-day VWAP)
- **Cash component:** $200,000
- Both payable within 45 Business Days of the Effective Date
- Shares subject to a **1-year lock-up period**

## 2. Development Milestone Payments (Section 6.2)
One-time payments tied to clinical/regulatory progress:
- $750,000 + $750,000 for first/last patient dosed in 1st Pivotal Trial, 1st Indication
- $375,000 + $375,000 for 1st Pivotal Trial, 2nd Indication
- $7,000,000 (1st US Approval) / $5,000,000 (2nd US Approval)
- $4,000,000 (1st ex-US Approval) / $2,000,000 (2nd ex-US Approval)

## 3. Sales Milestone Payments (Section 6.4)
Tiered one-time payments based on worldwide annual Net Sales thresholds, ranging from **$2.5M at $50M in sales** up to **$75M at $1.5B in sales**—only the highest tier reached in a year is paid.

## 4. Running Royalties (Section 6.5)
- **7.5%** royalty on aggregate worldwide annual Net Sales (as stated in the record, though labeled "seven percent (7.5%)")
- Reduced to 50% of that rate in countries lacking Regulatory Exclusivity and Valid Claims, subject to a **3% floor**
- Royalties creditable by 40% of Third-Party Patent License royalties paid, also subject to the 3% floor
- Royalty Term runs country-by-country/product-by-product until the latest of: patent expiration, 10th anniversary of first sale, or expiration of regulatory exclusivity — after which the license becomes **fully paid-up and perpetual**

## 5. Sublicense Revenue Share (Section 6.6(a))
Ocuphire receives **32% of any Sublicense Consideration** Processa receives from sublicensing the rights to third parties.

## 6. Cost Allocation
- Processa bears **100%** of Development, Commercialization, and patent prosecution/maintenance costs
- Processa must maintain minimum **$5M/occurrence–$10M aggregate** product liability insurance
- Late payments accrue interest at 30-day LIBOR + 5%

In short, the deal is structured as a **front-loaded stock+cash payment**, followed by a **success-based milestone ladder** (development and commercial), underpinned by a **tiered royalty stream with a floor**, plus a **share of any sublicensing revenue** Processa generates — a typical "hybrid" biopharma licensing payment structure.
